headline: The Bay invented its own sound three times (Fillmore psychedelia, Vallejo-Oakland hyphy, Filipino-American battle turntablism), and the Warriors' music credibility still lives across the bridge in The Town.
summary: Bay Area music has three homegrown movements a designer can draw on: 1960s psychedelic rock and the Fillmore poster art that came with it in San Francisco, the 'go dumb' hyphy movement of mid-2000s Vallejo and Oakland, and the turntablism that Filipino-American DJ crews built in Daly City and the Excelsior. The rap canon fans rep is overwhelmingly East Bay (Too $hort, Digital Underground, Hieroglyphics, Mac Dre, Keak da Sneak, E-40). The Warriors' own music ties grew up at Oracle Arena in Oakland and are carried today by courtside fixtures E-40 and MC Hammer and by longtime in-arena DJ D-Sharp. After a 37-45 season, with an aging Curry core running it back, music-led product can keep Dub Nation invested even if the standings don't. Build it with Oakland and Vallejo artists, Bay poster makers and Filipino-American DJs, launch it in their rooms, and license or skip every iconic asset.

insights.title: Hyphy and 'We Believe' are one memory
insights.detail: Hyphy, the hyperactive rap and dance movement built by Mac Dre, Keak da Sneak, Mistah F.A.B. and E-40, broke nationally with E-40's 'Tell Me When to Go' in 2006. That is the same window in which the 2007 'We Believe' Warriors, an 8 seed, knocked off 67-win Dallas in front of a roaring Oracle crowd.
insights.implication: For fans now in their 30s and 40s, hyphy's language and look are the soundtrack of their Warriors. That makes them the native vocabulary for an Oakland-heritage capsule, which should be built with Vallejo and Oakland artists rather than from a mood board.

insights.title: E-40 is Dub Nation's most visible celebrity fan
insights.detail: The Vallejo rapper has sat courtside since the Oracle years. When he was escorted out of Sacramento's Golden 1 Center during the 2023 Warriors-Kings playoff series, he called it racial profiling and the Bay rallied behind him.
insights.implication: He is the most credible bridge between the team and Bay rap, but he runs his own wine and spirits businesses (Earl Stevens Selections, Sluricane). Approach him as a paid co-creator with clear category boundaries, never as a cameo.

insights.title: The arena sound has a name: DJ D-Sharp
insights.detail: DJ D-Sharp, the Warriors' longtime in-arena DJ, carried the team's mix of Bay slaps and anthems from Oracle Arena to Chase Center. For many fans the in-game sound is his.
insights.implication: Make him the paid music curator for city drops. A licensed D-Sharp warmup mix as launch content gives product Bay credibility that a brand team cannot manufacture.

insights.title: Fillmore poster art is San Francisco's native graphic language
insights.detail: From 1966, Bill Graham's Fillmore posters by Wes Wilson, Victor Moscoso, Stanley Mouse and Alton Kelley, and Rick Griffin defined psychedelic design: hand-drawn letters swelling to fill a shape, and complementary colors that vibrate. The Fillmore still hands sold-out crowds a free commemorative poster, and the Warriors have kept the Haight connection alive with recurring Grateful Dead nights.
insights.implication: A numbered game-poster series drawn by living Bay poster artists is the most 'only San Francisco' visual a Warriors product can carry. Commission new work, and license archive art from its rights holders instead of tracing the classics.

insights.title: Battle turntablism is Bay-born and Filipino-American
insights.detail: Filipino-American mobile DJ crews in Daly City, San Francisco's Excelsior and the East Bay produced the Invisibl Skratch Piklz (DJ Qbert, Mix Master Mike, Shortkut), whose members won DMC world titles in the early 1990s and turned the turntable into an instrument. Pinole's P-Lo carries that lineage into today's rap production.
insights.implication: Turntable, slipmat and scratch-waveform graphics are earned Bay motifs and a natural story for Filipino American History Month in October and the Warriors' Filipino Heritage Night. Co-design the work with Filipino-American DJs, and credit and pay them.

insights.title: Oakland made the music; San Francisco has the address
insights.detail: Chase Center opened in Mission Bay in September 2019 with Metallica and the San Francisco Symphony, ending 47 years in Oakland, the city that produced most of the Bay rap canon. Many 'Town' fans, who also lost the Raiders and A's, still feel the move.
insights.implication: Music-led product should carry both 'The Town' and 'The City' and launch in Oakland rooms such as the Fox Theater. Product that only speaks Chase Center reads as tech-money San Francisco to the fan base's emotional core.

places.name: The Fillmore
places.why: Bill Graham's rock room since 1966, in the old 'Harlem of the West' jazz district, and still the place that gives sold-out crowds a free commemorative poster.

places.name: Fox Theater
places.why: A restored 1928 movie palace where Bay rap and R&B acts play their homecoming shows, which makes it the right Oakland stage for a Town product launch.

places.name: Oakland Arena (formerly Oracle Arena)
places.why: The 'Roaracle,' the Warriors' home for 47 years and the building where 'We Believe' happened; it still hosts concerts and remains a pilgrimage point for Oakland fans.

places.name: Chase Center and Thrive City
places.why: The current home court, opened in 2019 with Metallica and the SF Symphony; Thrive City's plaza is the natural stage for DJ-led launches on game days.

places.name: 924 Gilman Street
places.why: An all-ages, volunteer-run punk club since 1986 that launched Green Day, Operation Ivy and Rancid: the East Bay's DIY conscience.

places.name: Amoeba Music
places.why: The Bay's flagship record store, in a former bowling alley a few blocks from the Grateful Dead's old house, and the right door for a numbered poster-tee drop.

places.name: SFJAZZ Center
places.why: Billed as the first free-standing U.S. building made for jazz (2013), it carries forward the Fillmore jazz legacy that urban renewal destroyed.

places.name: KPOO 89.5 FM
places.why: A noncommercial community station on air since 1972, playing blues, jazz, gospel and hip-hop for Black San Francisco: a partner with deep roots, not reach.

places.name: 106 KMEL
places.why: For decades the Bay's hip-hop and R&B station and the dial where Bay rap and hyphy broke to a mass audience.

places.name: Sigmund Stern Grove
places.why: A eucalyptus-ringed natural amphitheater that has hosted free Sunday summer concerts since 1938, beloved across every Bay demographic.

people.name: E-40
people.role: Vallejo rapper, slang coiner and entrepreneur
people.why: The Warriors' most visible celebrity fan and an architect of mobb music and hyphy, with the authority to bless or sink a Bay music collab.

people.name: DJ D-Sharp
people.why: He has soundtracked games from Oracle to Chase Center, so he is the team's built-in music curator.

people.name: MC Hammer
people.role: East Oakland pop-rap superstar and former A's batboy
people.why: A courtside regular through the title years and a living symbol of Oakland's claim on the team.

people.name: Larry June
people.role: San Francisco rapper and independent label owner (The Freeminded Records)
people.why: His wellness-and-vintage-cars persona and his 2023 album with The Alchemist, 'The Great Escape,' make him the city's most respected current voice.

people.name: LaRussell
people.role: Vallejo rapper and independent operator (Good Compenny)
people.why: His backyard shows and fast, fan-owned release model are the new template for Bay independence; he is a natural co-creator if he has no conflicting deals.

people.name: P-Lo
people.role: Filipino-American rapper-producer from Pinole; HBK Gang member
people.why: He links the Bay's Filipino-American DJ lineage to current rap and is a credible voice for Filipino Heritage Night.

people.name: DJ Qbert
people.role: San Francisco turntablist; co-founder of the Invisibl Skratch Piklz
people.why: A DMC world champion and the global face of Bay turntablism, still teaching scratching worldwide.

people.name: Hieroglyphics
people.role: Oakland indie hip-hop collective (Del the Funky Homosapien, Souls of Mischief, Casual, Pep Love, Domino)
people.why: Behind '93 'til Infinity' and the Hiero Day festival, and holders of the third-eye logo, one of hip-hop's best-known collective marks.

moments.name: Carnaval San Francisco
moments.why: The Mission's Latin American and Caribbean music, dance and parade weekend, rooted in the neighborhood that raised Carlos Santana.

moments.name: Fillmore Jazz Festival
moments.why: A free street festival on Fillmore Street that honors the 'Harlem of the West' and fits naturally with a Fillmore poster-art story.

moments.name: Stern Grove Festival
moments.why: Free summer concerts with an all-ages crowd in the Sunset, an off-season way to keep the brand in front of families.

moments.name: Outside Lands
moments.why: The Bay's biggest ticketed festival and the summer's peak reach for previewing next season's city product.

moments.name: San Jose Jazz Summer Fest
moments.why: The South Bay's signature music weekend, a way into the Silicon Valley fan base that rarely sees Bay culture activations.

moments.name: Hiero Day
moments.why: Hieroglyphics' Oakland block-party festival is the pre-season gathering of East Bay hip-hop heads and an ideal seeding moment for a Town capsule.

moments.name: Hardly Strictly Bluegrass
moments.why: Warren Hellman's free Golden Gate Park festival, which draws hundreds of thousands just as preseason starts.

moments.name: Filipino American History Month and Warriors Filipino Heritage Night
moments.timing: October (heritage night date set each season)
moments.why: The best moment for a turntablism story co-created with Filipino-American DJs, in one of the country's largest Filipino-American communities.

vocabulary.meaning: Short for hyperactive: the mid-2000s Bay rap, dance and car-culture movement out of Vallejo and Oakland.
To lose yourself dancing, the core hyphy instruction, immortalized by E-40's 'Tell Me When to Go.'
The slow, funk-heavy, bass-driven 1990s Bay rap sound of Vallejo and Oakland (E-40 and The Click, Spice 1, Mac Mall).
Bay slang for a song that hits hard, rooted in trunk-rattling Bay beats and now used nationally.
Oakland and San Francisco respectively; every Bay music fan knows which side an artist reps.
The Bay Area ('Yay Area'), a common term in Bay rap lyrics.
The quintessential Northern California intensifier ('hella loud'), worn as a badge of Bay identity.
Mac Dre's term (and his Thizz Entertainment label), which refers to ecstasy. Know it, but keep it off product.

designCues.cue: Fillmore melt: hand-drawn letterforms that swell and warp to fill a shape
designCues.source: Wes Wilson's 1966-67 Fillmore posters, which set the template for psychedelic lettering.
designCues.use: Commission Bay letterers to draw 'Dub Nation' or 'The Bay' in this tradition for poster tees and hangtags. Do not copy or trace existing posters.

designCues.cue: Vibration orange set against Warriors Royal
designCues.source: Victor Moscoso's Fillmore-era optical clashes of equal-value complementary colors.
designCues.use: Use it as the single hit color against Warriors Royal (#1D428A) on poster prints, taping or an inside placket, tuned so the two vibrate. The hex is approximate, so match it with a lab dip.

designCues.cue: Scraper-bike candy foil: spokes wrapped in candy wrappers and colored foil tape
designCues.source: East Oakland's scraper-bike youth culture, put on the map by the Trunk Boiz' 2007 'Scraper Bike' video and the Original Scraper Bike Team.
designCues.use: Use iridescent foil-tape piping, spoke-pattern heat transfers and candy-color colorblocking, co-created with East Oakland scraper builders who are credited and paid.

designCues.source: The signature accessory of the hyphy era (Mac Dre, Keak da Sneak, E-40's 'Tell Me When to Go' video).
designCues.use: Use as a graphic icon or campaign styling for an Oakland-heritage capsule, paired with 'Go Dumb' type, never with 'Thizz' imagery.

designCues.source: Bay turntablism built by Filipino-American DJ crews and the Invisibl Skratch Piklz.
designCues.use: Print the waveform of a commissioned scratch routine by a named Bay DJ down a sleeve, cut slipmat-shaped hangtags, and credit the DJ on the tag.

designCues.cue: The Roaracle: crowd noise as heritage
designCues.source: Oracle Arena's reputation as the league's loudest building, peaking with the 2007 'We Believe' run.
designCues.use: Build a Town capsule around decibel-meter graphics and a waveform from licensed Oracle crowd audio in the team archive, and launch it in Oakland.

designCues.source: The Bay Bridge in the Warriors logo combined with the Bay's DJ culture.
designCues.use: Redraw the bridge as the line between two turntables labeled The Town and The City, as the chest graphic for a capsule that unites Oakland and San Francisco. The logo is team IP and requires NBA/team approval.

productHooks: A 'Go Dumb' Oakland-heritage capsule (shooting shirt, hoodie, crew socks) with scraper-foil piping and stunna-shade graphics, co-designed with Vallejo and Oakland artists such as LaRussell, launched at a Fox Theater show, with proceeds to an East Oakland youth music or bike program.

Numbered Fillmore-style poster tees for marquee nights (Oct. 21 at the Lakers, Dec. 25 vs. Denver), each drawn by a commissioned Bay poster artist and sold with a printed poster at Amoeba Haight and the Chase Center team store.

A turntablism capsule for October's Filipino American History Month and the Warriors' Filipino Heritage Night, with scratch-waveform sleeves and slipmat hangtags, co-created with Bay Filipino-American DJs (approach DJ Qbert or P-Lo) and launched with a Thrive City DJ set.
A DJ D-Sharp warmup tee for the home opener, carrying a QR code to a licensed D-Sharp Bay mix, sold at Thrive City.
A 'Roaracle' Town tee with a waveform of the 2007 'We Believe' crowd noise, sold in Oakland stores and at a Hiero Day or Oakland pop-up rather than only at Chase Center.
watchouts: Brand conflicts: Stephen Curry ended his Under Armour partnership in late 2025 (Curry Brand is independent) and his next partner is unconfirmed. Use him only through NBA-licensed assets in music content, and check every artist's apparel and beverage deals (E-40's spirits businesses included) before approaching them.

Third-party IP: Fillmore and Bill Graham archive posters, Grateful Dead marks (Steal Your Face, dancing bears), Hieroglyphics' third-eye logo, Thizz Entertainment marks, KMEL marks, and all song titles, lyrics and audio require licenses. Commission new art instead of tracing classics.

Hyphy-era imagery carries drug and danger references ('thizz,' ghost-riding, sideshows), and Oakland is actively cracking down on sideshows. Keep product to music, dance, stunna shades and scraper bikes.
Oakland's loss is real: the Warriors, Raiders and A's all left, so Oakland-nostalgia product without Oakland artists, Oakland launch venues and money back into Oakland will read as exploitation.

Filipino-American turntablism, Black Fillmore jazz history and Mission Latino music each belong to specific communities. Partner with them, credit them and pay them, and do not reduce any of them to a costume or a single stereotype.
